questions.q: Which malicious program can self-replicate across a network WITHOUT needing a host file or user action?
questions.solution: Worms travel and multiply on their own over network connections. Viruses need a host file, trojans need a user to install them and never self-replicate.
questions.shortcut: Worm = Wanders alone. If 'no host file / no user action' appears, it is a worm.

questions.q: In Excel, the intersection of a row and a column is called a:
questions.solution: A cell is the single box at a column-row crossing, addressed as ColumnLetter+RowNumber (e.g. B7). A range is a rectangular block of cells.
questions.shortcut: Spreadsheet atom = cell; address = letter + number.

questions.q: The default font of MS Word 2016 documents is:
questions.solution: From Word 2007 to 2021 the default body font is Calibri 11 pt (Times New Roman 12 was the Word 2003 default; Office 365 moved to Aptos 12 in 2023).
questions.shortcut: Eras: 2003 Times New Roman 12 -> 2007-21 Calibri 11 -> 2023+ Aptos 12.

questions.q: EPROM differs from PROM because it can be erased by:
questions.solution: EPROM (Erasable Programmable ROM) is erased by exposing the quartz window to ultraviolet light. PROM cannot be erased once programmed; EEPROM is the electrically erasable version.
questions.shortcut: One E = light (EPROM, UV); two E's = electricity (EEPROM).

questions.q: In the passage, 'no paid leave cushions an illness' suggests that an ill gig worker:
options: has no paid protection to fall back on when sick
must train others during sick leave
receives special leave reserved for illness
gets paid compensation from the platform
questions.solution: The sentence lists absences: no minimum wage for waiting hours, no paid leave, pension contributions fully self-funded. *Cushions* here = softens the blow / provides a protective layer — so the sick worker has no paid buffer. (a) and (b) contradict the sentence (paid leave/compensation is exactly what is missing). (d) misreads cushion as a job duty — nothing about training appears.
questions.shortcut: Own-words first: 'cushions an illness' = *protects against the money lost when sick*. Then match.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (3).
questions.solution: The clause after the semicolon supplies the meaning: twenty minutes on Sunday cannot undo six days of sitting — benefits depend on doing it **regularly**. The noun naming that idea is *regularity*. *Equipment* contradicts the earlier line that the walk demands no equipment; luck and medicine are outside the sentence's logic.
questions.shortcut: Name the missing idea first ('consistency'), then match — the option echoing the next clause is the answer.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

Who taught you English?
options: By whom were you taught English?
By whom you were taught English?
Whom were taught English by you?
questions.solution: Who-questions passivise to **By whom + auxiliary + subject**: 'By whom were you taught English?' B keeps 'who' instead of 'by whom'; C uses statement word order; D scrambles the clause entirely.
questions.shortcut: Who → By whom + aux + subject; word order is the trap.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

The gardener is watering the plants.
options: The plants are watered by the gardener.
The plants are being watered by the gardener.
The plants are being water by the gardener.
The plants is being watered by the gardener.
questions.solution: Present continuous → **are being + V3** with the plural new subject 'the plants'. B uses V1; C fails number agreement (is for plants); D drops 'being', turning it into simple present.
questions.shortcut: are being + V3 — check the V3 and the number both.

questions.q: ***Ain-i-Akbari***, the detailed account of Akbar's administration, was written by —
questions.solution: **Abul Fazl** wrote the *Akbarnama*, whose third volume is the *Ain-i-Akbari*. Faizi was his brother (poet); Badauni wrote the critical *Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh*.
questions.shortcut: **A**bul = **A**in = **A**kbarnama.

questions.q: The men's singles title at Wimbledon 2026 was won by —
questions.solution: Top seed **Jannik Sinner** of Italy beat second seed Alexander Zverev in the final. Zverev is the runner-up option, not the champion.
questions.shortcut: Wimbledon 2026: Sinner over Zverev — an all top-2-seed final.

questions.q: **Amir Khusrau**, the poet called *Tuti-i-Hind*, was a disciple of which Sufi saint?
questions.solution: Amir Khusrau was the devoted disciple of **Nizamuddin Auliya** of the Chishti order in Delhi; both are buried in the Nizamuddin dargah complex. Bahauddin Zakariya was a Suhrawardi saint of Multan; Sirhindi was Naqshbandi.
questions.shortcut: Both are in Delhi's **Nizamuddin** — the disciple rests beside his master.

questions.q: In the **Battle of Haldighati (1576)**, the Mughal army that fought Maharana Pratap was commanded by —
questions.solution: **Raja Man Singh** of Amber led Akbar's army at Haldighati. Bairam Khan was Akbar's regent at Panipat II; Todar Mal was the revenue expert.
questions.shortcut: Haldighati = Rajput vs Rajput: Pratap vs **Man Singh**.

questions.q: The radius of a circular field is 21 m. The cost of fencing it at ₹10 per metre is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
questions.solution: Circumference $=2\times\frac{22}{7}\times21=132$ m. Cost $=132\times10=$ ₹1,320.
questions.shortcut: $132$ m → ₹1320. Trap: ₹13,860 uses area ($\pi r^2$) instead of circumference.

questions.q: The fourth proportional to 4, 9 and 12 is:
A alone completes a work in 12 days and B alone in 18 days. They work together and receive ₹840 as total wages. A's share is:
questions.shortcut: Equal days ⇒ wage ratio = rate ratio = 3 : 2.

questions.q: The minimum value of $4\tan^2\theta+9\cot^2\theta$ (for acute $\theta$) is:
questions.solution:
By AM–GM, $4\tan^2\theta+9\cot^2\theta\ge2\sqrt{4\times9}=12$,

with equality when $2\tan\theta=3\cot\theta$, i.e. $\tan^2\theta=\frac32$ (reachable since tan is unbounded).
questions.shortcut: $2\sqrt{ab}=2\sqrt{36}=12$. Trap: 6 is $\sqrt{ab}$ (forgot to double), 13 is $a+b$.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 59 59" width="59" height="59" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="4,21 38,21 38,55 4,55"/><polygon points="4,21 38,21 55,4 21,4"/><polygon points="38,21 55,4 55,38 38,55"/><text x="21" y="43" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">3</text><text x="29.5" y="16.5" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">2</text><text x="46.5" y="33.5" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-family="sans-serif">4</text></svg>
questions.solution: Opposite pairs: in the row 2, 3, 4, 5 → 2 ↔ 4 and 3 ↔ 5; the leftovers 1 ↔ 6. So a cube showing 1 with 6, or 2 with 4, is impossible. Between the two cubes with 1, 3, 4: fold with 3 facing you — 1 (attached above 2, which folds to the left) comes over the top, and 4 folds to the right. So 1 on top, 3 in front, 4 on the right is correct; the version with 4 in front and 3 on the right has the reverse order.
questions.shortcut: Reject opposite pairs first, then check the corner order.

questions.solution: Folded along the top-left to bottom-right diagonal. Each punch is reflected across that diagonal (swap its horizontal and vertical distances): the hole near the middle of the left edge reappears near the middle of the top edge; the one near the bottom-left corner reappears near the top-right side. Final: **4 holes**.
questions.shortcut: Main diagonal: (x, y) ↔ (y, x).

questions.q: In a certain code, **LOTUS** is written as **MNUTT**. Which of the following is the code for **TULIP**?
questions.solution: LOTUS → MNUTT: L→M (+1), O→N (−1), T→U (+1), U→T (−1), S→T (+1). Vowels move −1, consonants move +1. TULIP: T+1 = U, U−1 = T, L+1 = M, I−1 = H, P+1 = Q → **UTMHQ**.
questions.shortcut: The vowels are the letters that went backwards — spot them first.

questions.solution: Two elements. Shading moves **anticlockwise**: TL → BL → BR → TR → next **TL**. The arrow turns **90° clockwise**: up-right → down-right → down-left → up-left → next **up-right**. The answer has the top-left quarter shaded and the arrow pointing up-right.
questions.shortcut: Shading and arrow separately.
